items.prompt: What does a metric tell you that a single log line cannot?
choices: Exactly what happened to one request
How the system is doing in aggregate, such as an error rate
items.explanation: Metrics summarize behavior across all requests (rates, percentiles). A single log line describes one event.

items.prompt: Which signal best answers 'what exactly happened to this one request, and why?'
items.explanation: Logs are per-event records with the detail needed to explain one request.

items.prompt: Which signal shows where, across services, a request spent its time?
items.explanation: A trace links the work done by each service for one request into a timeline.

items.prompt: In the L1 scenario, what was missing from production?
choices: Logs, metrics, and traces all in useful form
items.explanation: There was no usable structured log, no dashboard of how widespread the failure was, and no trace of the path through the four services.

items.prompt: An alert says 'checkout error rate is 2.1%'. Which signal produced it?
items.explanation: An error rate is an aggregate number tracked over time, which is a metric.

items.prompt: Why does a system with good observability avoid the 'add print statement, redeploy, wait' loop?
choices: It can answer new questions from data it already records
It runs a debugger in production
items.explanation: Observability means questions can be answered from existing telemetry, without shipping new code first.

items.prompt: Which question is a trace best suited for?
choices: How many requests per second are we serving?
What was the exact error message for order 8841?
Which of the four services made checkout slow?
items.explanation: Cross-service latency attribution is exactly what a trace shows.

items.prompt: In practice, which order are the signals usually used during an incident?
choices: Metrics to notice, traces to narrow, logs to explain
items.explanation: A metric alert says something is wrong, a trace narrows it to a service, and that service's logs give the detail.

items.prompt: Checkout p99 latency doubled at 14:02. Which signal tells you THAT it happened, and which tells you WHERE?
choices: Logs tell that, metrics tell where
Metrics tell that, traces tell where
items.explanation: Metrics show the aggregate change over time; a trace of a slow request shows which service consumed the time.
items.reflection: Logs, metrics, and traces each answer a different question about the same system. Where else do you rely on several complementary views of one thing: a car's dashboard gauge, a mechanic's inspection report, and the route your GPS recorded, say? What would you lose if you only had one?

items.prompt: A dashboard shows 0.1% errors, but one VIP customer's order failed. Why might the metric not reveal it, and what would?
choices: The aggregate hides one request; that request's logs or trace would show it
Metrics are always wrong; use none
Only restarting the service would reveal it
items.explanation: Aggregates smooth out single events. Per-request detail lives in logs and traces.
items.reflection: Logs, metrics, and traces each answer a different question about the same system. Where else do you rely on several complementary views of one thing: a car's dashboard gauge, a mechanic's inspection report, and the route your GPS recorded, say? What would you lose if you only had one?

items.prompt: A team says 'we have great logs, we don't need metrics.' What can't they easily answer?
choices: Whether 1% or 90% of checkouts are failing right now, cheaply and quickly
items.explanation: Counting across millions of log lines is slow and expensive; metrics are built to answer 'how much, how often' cheaply.
items.reflection: Logs, metrics, and traces each answer a different question about the same system. Where else do you rely on several complementary views of one thing: a car's dashboard gauge, a mechanic's inspection report, and the route your GPS recorded, say? What would you lose if you only had one?

items.prompt: What is a structured log line?
choices: A line with a timestamp only
A machine-parseable record (usually JSON) with consistent fields
items.explanation: Structured means consistent, parseable fields rather than prose.

items.prompt: Why is console.log('here') hard to use in production?
choices: There is nothing to filter on except the literal text
items.explanation: Free text can't be filtered by service, level, or request.

items.prompt: Which query is easy only against structured logs?
choices: Show every error from payment-service where attempt >= 3
items.explanation: Field-based filtering depends on fields existing.

items.prompt: Which field in the example record ties a log to one request?
items.explanation: requestId identifies the request across all log lines for it.

items.prompt: Which format is almost always used for structured logs?
items.explanation: JSON is the common machine-parseable choice.

items.prompt: Which is better as a structured field than buried in the message text?
items.explanation: Putting values in their own fields lets you filter and aggregate on them.

items.prompt: Structured logging mainly helps with:
choices: Searching and aggregating across millions of lines
items.explanation: Its value is queryability at scale.

items.prompt: A structured record usually includes a timestamp so that:
choices: Events can be ordered and time-bounded
items.explanation: Timestamps allow ordering and time-window queries.

items.prompt: A team logs 'Payment failed for order 8841 after 3 retries'. What's the main weakness versus a structured record?
choices: orderId and retry count can't be filtered or aggregated as fields
items.explanation: The values are embedded in prose; you would need fragile text parsing to query them.
items.reflection: Structured logs turn free text into fields you can filter and aggregate. Where else does giving information consistent fields (a spreadsheet instead of a paragraph, a form instead of a letter) make it far easier to search or combine?

items.prompt: Two services log the same event with different field names ('reqId' vs 'requestId'). What breaks?
choices: Cross-service queries by one field name miss half the lines
items.explanation: Structure only pays off when field names are consistent across services.
items.reflection: Structured logs turn free text into fields you can filter and aggregate. Where else does giving information consistent fields (a spreadsheet instead of a paragraph, a form instead of a letter) make it far easier to search or combine?

items.prompt: Which field is dangerous to put into structured logs without care?
choices: A raw credit card number or password
items.explanation: Structured fields are easy to search and ship around, so secrets in them spread widely; sensitive data should be redacted.
items.reflection: Structured logs turn free text into fields you can filter and aggregate. Where else does giving information consistent fields (a spreadsheet instead of a paragraph, a form instead of a letter) make it far easier to search or combine?

items.prompt: Which level fits 'a retry succeeded after one failure'?
items.explanation: Something unexpected happened but the system recovered on its own: warn.

items.prompt: Which level fits 'the payment call failed and the customer saw an error'?
items.explanation: An operation failed and someone is affected: error.

items.prompt: Which level fits 'the process cannot continue and is about to exit'?
items.explanation: fatal means the process itself cannot continue.

items.prompt: Which level is usually off in production because of volume?
items.explanation: debug is fine-grained and high-volume.

items.prompt: What is a typical production threshold?
items.explanation: info and above, with debug enabled narrowly and temporarily.

items.prompt: Which level fits 'request completed in 120ms'?
items.explanation: A routine event worth a permanent record is info.

items.prompt: Why not log everything at the same level?
choices: Important lines get lost among routine ones
It uses more disk by design
items.explanation: Without severity, you can't separate the signal from routine noise.

items.prompt: The ordering from lowest to highest severity is:
items.explanation: debug < info < warn < error < fatal.

items.prompt: A fallback cache is used because the primary database timed out, and the request still succeeds. Best level?
items.explanation: The system recovered, but the primary failing is worth attention: warn.
items.reflection: Levels rank events by how much attention they deserve. Where else do you triage by severity: hospital triage, email priority flags, a to-do list? What goes wrong when everything is marked urgent?

items.prompt: An engineer enables debug logging for all services in production 'just in case'. What is the main risk?
choices: Services stop responding to requests by design
Volume and cost explode and the real signals drown
items.explanation: Debug everywhere is a haystack; enable it narrowly (one service, one request, short window).
items.reflection: Levels rank events by how much attention they deserve. Where else do you triage by severity: hospital triage, email priority flags, a to-do list? What goes wrong when everything is marked urgent?

items.prompt: A single validation failure from a user typing a bad email: error or something lower?
choices: Usually not error; it's expected input handling (info/warn)
Always error because it's a failure
items.explanation: Errors should mean the system failed to do something it should have. Expected rejections shouldn't page anyone or inflate error rates.
items.reflection: Levels rank events by how much attention they deserve. Where else do you triage by severity: hospital triage, email priority flags, a to-do list? What goes wrong when everything is marked urgent?

items.prompt: What problem does a correlation ID solve?
choices: Linking log lines from many services to one request
items.explanation: It lets you filter all services' logs by one request.

items.prompt: Where is the correlation ID generated?
choices: At the point the request enters the system
items.explanation: It is created at the entry point (the gateway) and passed on.

items.prompt: How does the ID reach downstream services?
choices: Passed along on each call, e.g. in a header
items.explanation: It must physically travel with each call.

items.prompt: What is a span?
choices: One unit of work inside a trace, with start, end and parent
items.explanation: Spans are the individual units of work that make up a trace.

items.prompt: What does a trace ID identify?
items.explanation: All spans of one request share a trace ID.

items.prompt: What does a span's parent reference allow?
items.explanation: Parent references are how the nesting is reconstructed.

items.prompt: If a service drops the trace ID on an outbound call, what happens?
choices: The downstream work is orphaned from the trace
items.explanation: The downstream logs/spans can't be connected to that request.

items.prompt: A trace viewer mostly shows:
items.explanation: It renders spans as a nested timeline, showing where time went.

items.prompt: Gateway logs have requestId req_8841, but payment logs use a freshly generated ID. What is the effect?
choices: The two log streams can't be joined by ID
items.explanation: A service that makes its own ID instead of reusing the incoming one breaks the thread.
items.reflection: A correlation ID turns many independent records into one story by threading a shared key through them. Where else does a shared reference number tie scattered pieces together: a parcel tracking number, a support ticket across emails and calls? What breaks when one handoff forgets the number?

items.prompt: A trace shows gateway 1200ms total, with payment.charge 900ms of which gateway.call is 870ms. Where should you look first?
choices: The outbound call to the payment gateway
items.explanation: The deepest long span, gateway.call, accounts for nearly all the time.
items.reflection: A correlation ID turns many independent records into one story by threading a shared key through them. Where else does a shared reference number tie scattered pieces together: a parcel tracking number, a support ticket across emails and calls? What breaks when one handoff forgets the number?

items.prompt: Why is a flat requestId less informative than a trace with spans, even if both link the logs?
choices: It links lines but doesn't capture timing and parent/child structure
items.explanation: A flat ID joins events; spans add duration and call hierarchy.
items.reflection: A correlation ID turns many independent records into one story by threading a shared key through them. Where else does a shared reference number tie scattered pieces together: a parcel tracking number, a support ticket across emails and calls? What breaks when one handoff forgets the number?

items.prompt: Which metric type only ever goes up?
items.explanation: A counter is cumulative: total requests, total errors.

items.prompt: Which type fits 'current queue depth'?
items.explanation: A gauge goes up and down and reports a current value.

items.prompt: Which type lets you ask for p99 latency?
items.explanation: Histograms record a distribution so percentiles can be computed.

items.prompt: Which type fits 'total errors since start'?
items.explanation: Cumulative totals are counters.

items.prompt: What does 'p99 = 340ms' mean?
choices: 99% of requests were at or below 340ms
items.explanation: A percentile says what fraction of values fall at or below a threshold.

items.prompt: Why are metrics cheap to store?
items.explanation: They keep only aggregates, not individual events.

items.prompt: Which type fits 'open database connections right now'?
items.explanation: It rises and falls, so it's a gauge.

items.prompt: Metrics answer:
items.explanation: Aggregates answer volume and rate questions; logs and traces answer which and why.

items.prompt: A dashboard shows average latency 80ms, yet users complain of slowness. What metric would expose the problem?
items.explanation: Averages hide the slow tail; a percentile from a histogram shows it.
items.reflection: Counter, gauge, and histogram are three ways of keeping a number over time. Where else do you pick the right measuring tool: an odometer, a fuel gauge, a lap-time distribution? What would you misread if you used the wrong one?

items.prompt: A counter reads 1,000,000. Is that good or bad?
choices: Not meaningful alone; you need its rate over time
items.explanation: Counters are cumulative totals; their rate of change is what's informative.
items.reflection: Counter, gauge, and histogram are three ways of keeping a number over time. Where else do you pick the right measuring tool: an odometer, a fuel gauge, a lap-time distribution? What would you misread if you used the wrong one?

items.prompt: Someone models 'active connections' as a counter. What goes wrong?
choices: It can't decrease, so it only reports total connections ever opened
items.explanation: Counters only increase; a value that goes down needs a gauge.
items.reflection: Counter, gauge, and histogram are three ways of keeping a number over time. Where else do you pick the right measuring tool: an odometer, a fuel gauge, a lap-time distribution? What would you misread if you used the wrong one?

items.prompt: What is a metric's cardinality?
choices: Number of unique label-value combinations (time series)
items.explanation: Each unique label combination is a separate time series.

items.prompt: A counter with no labels is how many time series?
items.explanation: No labels means a single series.

items.prompt: Which label is low-cardinality?
items.explanation: Status codes have only a handful of values.

items.prompt: Which label is dangerously high-cardinality?
items.explanation: Millions of users means millions of series.

items.prompt: Where should per-request detail like requestId live?
items.explanation: Logs and traces are built for per-event detail.

items.prompt: Labels statusCode (~10) and route (~40) give roughly how many series?
items.explanation: Series multiply: 10 x 40 = 400.

items.prompt: Why is high cardinality a problem?
choices: It creates a huge number of time series that cost storage and query time
items.explanation: Each series is stored and indexed separately.

items.prompt: Adding a label to a metric multiplies series count by:
choices: The number of distinct values the label can take
items.explanation: Series count grows by the product of distinct values.

items.prompt: Which label is the safest to add to a request-count metric?
items.explanation: A small, bounded set of values keeps cardinality manageable.
items.reflection: Cardinality is the number of distinct label combinations a metric must track. Where else does adding one more way to slice things multiply the work: filing cabinets with a folder per customer, a spreadsheet tab per day? When is the extra slicing worth it?

items.prompt: A metric has 400 series. A new label with 50,000 distinct values is added. Roughly how many series result?
items.explanation: 400 x 50,000 = 20,000,000, which is why the blow-up is so sudden.
items.reflection: Cardinality is the number of distinct label combinations a metric must track. Where else does adding one more way to slice things multiply the work: filing cabinets with a folder per customer, a spreadsheet tab per day? When is the extra slicing worth it?

items.prompt: You need to find which user experienced an error. Should you add userId as a metric label?
choices: No; use logs or traces keyed by user/request for per-user lookup
items.explanation: Per-user questions belong in per-event signals, not low-cardinality aggregates.
items.reflection: Cardinality is the number of distinct label combinations a metric must track. Where else does adding one more way to slice things multiply the work: filing cabinets with a folder per customer, a spreadsheet tab per day? When is the extra slicing worth it?

items.prompt: When should a logger check the level?
items.explanation: The check goes first so dropped lines cost almost nothing.

items.prompt: What does a logger do with a debug line when the threshold is info?
items.explanation: debug rank 10 < info 20, so it is dropped.

items.prompt: Which level ranks highest?
items.explanation: fatal = 50 is highest in the example scale.

items.prompt: Why does filtering early matter at scale?
choices: Saves CPU on lines that get discarded
items.explanation: Serializing millions of lines to discard them is wasted work.

items.prompt: With threshold warn (30), which of these are written?
items.explanation: Everything at rank 30 or above is written.

items.prompt: The level check is typically a:
items.explanation: Each level has a numeric rank; compare to the threshold.

items.prompt: Lowering the threshold to debug will:
items.explanation: More levels pass the filter, so volume rises.

items.prompt: Which operation does the early return avoid?
choices: Timestamp creation, field merging, and JSON serialization
items.explanation: Those are the costs of building a record.

items.prompt: A caller writes logger.debug(JSON.stringify(bigObject)) with threshold info. Where is the cost paid?
choices: In the caller, before the logger can check the level
items.explanation: The argument is built before the call, so the filter can't save it.
items.reflection: Level filtering saves work by deciding early whether to pay for the rest. Where else does an early cheap check avoid an expensive step: a bouncer checking IDs before the venue prepares a table, a spam filter running before full content analysis?

items.prompt: Which design avoids paying for expensive debug arguments?
choices: Passing a lazy callback or raw fields so the logger serializes only if enabled
items.explanation: Deferring the expensive work until after the level check avoids it.
items.reflection: Level filtering saves work by deciding early whether to pay for the rest. Where else does an early cheap check avoid an expensive step: a bouncer checking IDs before the venue prepares a table, a spam filter running before full content analysis?

items.prompt: Production threshold is info, and you need debug for one failing request. Best approach?
choices: Enable debug narrowly (one service/request, short window)
items.explanation: Targeted, temporary debug gives detail without the volume cost.
items.reflection: Level filtering saves work by deciding early whether to pay for the rest. Where else does an early cheap check avoid an expensive step: a bouncer checking IDs before the venue prepares a table, a spam filter running before full content analysis?

items.prompt: How does a trace viewer know span B is nested inside span A?
items.explanation: Nesting comes from the parent reference.

items.prompt: Which span has no parent?
items.explanation: The root span (e.g. gateway.handle) has no parent.

items.prompt: What do all spans of one request share?
items.explanation: traceId groups spans; spanId is unique per span.

items.prompt: Which field is unique per span?
items.explanation: Each span has its own spanId.

items.prompt: A span tree is analogous to:
items.explanation: Parent/child spans mirror nested calls, but are stored.

items.prompt: What carries the trace context between services?
items.explanation: Context must be propagated across each boundary.

items.prompt: Inside one process, which facility can carry context implicitly?
items.explanation: Runtime facilities like AsyncLocalStorage can pass it behind the scenes.

items.prompt: A span records:
choices: Start time, end time, name, and parent
items.explanation: Timing plus identity plus parent make the tree and timeline possible.

items.prompt: A span is given the wrong parentSpanId. What is the most likely symptom?
choices: A plausible-looking trace that attributes work to the wrong caller
items.explanation: A wrong parent quietly misrepresents who called what.
items.reflection: A span tree is rebuilt from nothing but each span's pointer to its parent. Where else is a hierarchy encoded by child-to-parent pointers: a file system's folders, an org chart, reply threads in a comment section? What happens to the picture if one pointer is wrong?

items.prompt: A span's parentSpanId refers to a span that was never reported (a service dropped telemetry). How does the viewer typically show it?
choices: As an orphan or with a gap, since the parent is missing
items.explanation: Without the parent record, the tree has a hole.
items.reflection: A span tree is rebuilt from nothing but each span's pointer to its parent. Where else is a hierarchy encoded by child-to-parent pointers: a file system's folders, an org chart, reply threads in a comment section? What happens to the picture if one pointer is wrong?

items.prompt: Two sibling calls made in parallel under one parent overlap in time. Is that a wrong tree?
choices: No, siblings can overlap when work runs in parallel
items.explanation: Parallel children of one parent are valid and often expected.
items.reflection: A span tree is rebuilt from nothing but each span's pointer to its parent. Where else is a hierarchy encoded by child-to-parent pointers: a file system's folders, an org chart, reply threads in a comment section? What happens to the picture if one pointer is wrong?

items.prompt: What is the goal of sampling logs/traces?
choices: Reduce volume while keeping what matters
items.explanation: Cut cost while preserving the important cases.

items.prompt: In the hybrid rule, what happens to a failed request?
items.explanation: Failures are never dropped.

items.prompt: What happens to successful requests under the hybrid rule?
items.explanation: A small random fraction is kept.

items.prompt: Head sampling decides:
items.explanation: Head means the beginning of the request.

items.prompt: Tail sampling decides:
choices: After the request finishes, using its outcome
items.explanation: It looks at the result before deciding.

items.prompt: What is the cost of tail sampling?
choices: Buffering every in-flight trace until it ends
items.explanation: It has to hold traces in memory until a decision can be made.

items.prompt: At 40M lines/day, why sample?
items.explanation: Storing every routine success is mostly wasted spend.

items.prompt: Why is a very low head-sampling rate risky without error handling?
items.explanation: Failures are thinned out at the same rate as successes.

items.prompt: With 1% head sampling and no error rule, what fraction of failures is kept?
items.explanation: Head sampling can't tell a future failure from a success.
items.reflection: Sampling trades completeness for cost by deciding what is worth keeping. Where else do you keep a representative slice but never discard the exceptions: quality inspection of a factory line, a poll of voters, auditing a sample of receipts? What would make you inspect everything instead?

items.prompt: A request succeeds but takes 5 seconds. Which approach can still keep it as interesting?
items.explanation: Only a decision made after the request finishes can use its duration.
items.reflection: Sampling trades completeness for cost by deciding what is worth keeping. Where else do you keep a representative slice but never discard the exceptions: quality inspection of a factory line, a poll of voters, auditing a sample of receipts? What would make you inspect everything instead?

items.prompt: Service A keeps a trace and service B drops the same request because they sample independently. Result?
items.explanation: Sampling decisions should be made once and propagated so all services agree.
items.reflection: Sampling trades completeness for cost by deciding what is worth keeping. Where else do you keep a representative slice but never discard the exceptions: quality inspection of a factory line, a poll of voters, auditing a sample of receipts? What would make you inspect everything instead?
